item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports adaptive intent fusion, although explicit boundary detection is less established in these results. [HM4SR (WWW 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.14269) introduces timestamp-conditioned temporal mixture-of-experts alongside modality selection; useful architectural inspiration, but its multimodal inputs and category supervision exceed this task’s available data. [DSASR (2026)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-02282-0) directly separates short- and long-term causal transformers, using cosine-distance preference drift to gate their combination; its demographic conditioning would require replacement with observable history features. [ICSRec (WSDM 2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3616855.3635773) learns latent intents from sliding subsequences through coarse/fine contrastive objectives without explicit intent labels. These methods model changing preferences but do not establish learned session boundaries.\n\nFor lightweight SASRec adaptation, [session-aware methods (2025)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/10902109) add session tokens, segment embeddings, or temporal self-attention with little parameter overhead; incorporating session information is distinct from discovering boundaries. [SURE, an ICLR 2026 submission](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=htIO088ZZF), uses loss-based change-point detection and Hedge-weighted experts, but targets calibrated recommendation sets rather than fixed top-10 ranking. Practical synthesis—not a published result: retain SASRec, add several causal recency/decay experts, and learn prefix-dependent routing from timestamp gaps, recent-versus-long-term embedding disagreement, and recent interaction coherence. This could let concentrated recent activity outweigh stale history without imposing one universal window. Train gates solely on observed training prefixes; select configurations by macro validation HR@10. Any change-point feature must likewise use only already-observed interactions."}
